steps.body: Every count of tenths has a decimal name. The digit after the decimal point counts the tenths.
steps.narration: Every count of tenths has a decimal name. The digit after the decimal point counts the tenths.

widget.prompt: Shade the strip to show 0.5. Each column is one tenth.

commonCounts.feedback: The count of shaded columns must match the tenths digit of 0.5 — that digit is 5, so 5 columns.

widget.successFeedback: Exactly 5 of the 10 columns — 5 tenths, which the decimal writes as 0.5.
widget.lowFeedback: The shaded amount is still below the target. Each column is one tenth — count the shaded columns against the decimal.
widget.highFeedback: The shaded amount has gone past the target. Each column is one tenth — count the shaded columns against the decimal.

predict.prompt: You will shade 5 of the 10 columns. Which decimal will name the shaded amount?
predict.reveal: Five columns is 5 tenths. The decimal puts that 5 directly after the point: 0.5. Writing 0.05 would put the 5 in the hundredths place — 5 single cells out of 100, only half a column.

explanationVariants: Each column is one tenth, so 5 columns writes as 0.5.

widget.prompt: A unit square is split into 10 equal columns, and 5 of them are shaded. Write the shaded amount as a decimal.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the count of shaded columns, and a count of parts is a whole number. Each column is one tenth of the square, so 5 columns is 5 tenths, written with the 5 in the tenths place.
That puts the 5 in the hundredths place, which would mean 5 cells of a hundred-cell grid. This square has only 10 columns, so each shaded column is a tenth of the whole.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Each column is one tenth of the square. Count the shaded columns and write that count in the tenths place, directly after the decimal point.

explanationVariants: The 9 sits in the tenths place, so the fraction is 9/10.

widget.prompt: Which fraction names the same amount as 0.9?

options.feedback: Correct — the digit 9 sits in the tenths place, so 0.9 means 9 of 10 equal parts.
A denominator of 100 would mean 9 hundredths, written 0.09. The digit 9 in 0.9 sits one place higher — in the tenths place.
That fraction has the part count and the number of equal pieces swapped. The decimal names 9 pieces out of 10 equal pieces, so 9 belongs on top.
A denominator of 1 would make this 9 whole units. The decimal point in 0.9 says the amount is less than one whole, cut into 10 equal parts.
